**The Weight of a Thousand Words**

The first word is always the hardest. It sits on the tip of your tongue, heavy with possibility, trembling with the weight of what follows. A thousand words—how much can they hold? A story? A confession? A warning? A love letter? A manifesto? A scream?

I’ve never been good at silence. Words spill from me like water from a broken faucet, relentless, sometimes messy, but always there. They are my shield, my weapon, my confession booth. They are the way I make sense of the world, even when the world makes no sense at all.

A thousand words. That’s roughly the length of a short story. Or a long letter. Or a manifesto. Or a rant. Or a eulogy. Or a love letter. Or a warning. Or a scream.

I could write about the time I almost died. The way the world slowed down as the car skidded, the way my breath hitched, the way I thought, *This is it.* And then—nothing. Just the sound of my own heartbeat, too loud in my ears, and the realization that I was still here. That the universe had decided, for now, that I wasn’t done.

I could write about love. The way it sneaks up on you, the way it makes your stomach flip and your hands shake. The way it feels like a secret you can’t keep, a fire you can’t contain. The way it burns bright and then, sometimes, fades into something quieter, something deeper. Or the way it can turn to ash in your hands, leaving you with nothing but the memory of its warmth.

I could write about grief. The way it sits in your chest like a stone, heavy and unyielding. The way it makes time stretch and warp, so that days feel like years and years feel like seconds. The way it makes you question everything—your faith, your purpose, your very existence. The way it lingers, long after the tears have dried.

I could write about the future. The way it looms, both terrifying and exhilarating. The way it feels like a blank page, waiting to be filled. The way it makes you wonder—what if? What if I had made a different choice? What if I had said yes instead of no? What if I had stayed instead of left? What if I had tried instead of given up?

A thousand words. That’s roughly the length of a confession. Or a manifesto. Or a scream.

I could write about the things I’ve done. The things I regret. The things I’m proud of. The things I wish I could take back. The things I wish I could do again. The things I wish I had the courage to do.

I could write about the things I’ve seen. The beauty and the horror. The kindness and the cruelty. The moments that took my breath away. The moments that broke me.

I could write about the things I’ve learned. That life is fragile. That love is rare. That time is fleeting. That pain is inevitable, but so is joy. That we are all, in the end, just trying to make sense of it all.

A thousand words. That’s roughly the length of a love letter. Or a warning. Or a scream.

I could write about the things I fear. The things that keep me up at night. The things that make my heart race. The things that make me question everything.

I could write about the things I hope for. The things I dream about. The things I long for. The things I believe in.

I could write about the things I know. That we are all connected. That we are all alone. That we are all searching. That we are all lost.

A thousand words. That’s roughly the length of a story. Or a confession. Or a scream.

I could write about the things I’ve lost. The people, the places, the moments. The things that are gone forever. The things that haunt me. The things that shape me.

I could write about the things I’ve found. The people, the places, the moments. The things that saved me. The things that changed me.

I could write about the things I’m still searching for. The answers, the meaning, the purpose. The things that elude me. The things that drive me.

A thousand words. That’s roughly the length of a manifesto. Or a warning. Or a scream.

I could write about the things I believe in. The things that give me hope. The things that keep me going. The things that make me fight.

I could write about the things I doubt. The things that make me question. The things that make me afraid.

I could write about the things I know for certain. That life is short. That love is worth it. That pain is temporary. That joy is fleeting. That we are all, in the end, just trying to make sense of it all.

A thousand words. That’s roughly the length of a scream.

And so, I write. Because words are all I have. Because words are all I need. Because words are the only way I know how to make sense of the world, even when the world makes no sense at all.

And so, I write. A thousand words. And then, perhaps, a thousand more.
